chunk_findings.detail: `urllib.request.build_opener(_HTTPHandler, _HTTPSHandler)` passes the handler classes, not instances. `OpenerDirector.add_handler` expects an instance and invokes `handler.add_parent(self)`; when `handler` is a class this raises `TypeError` (`add_parent() missing 1 required positional argument: 'parent'`). Concrete input: `UrllibHttpClient().request("GET", "http://example.com", timeout=1, on_connect=lambda c: None)` crashes before any request is sent, so the socket-abort path is completely broken and the error is not an `HttpError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:_tracked_opener

chunk_findings.detail: `urllib.parse.urlsplit(url)` runs outside the `try` block and raises `ValueError` for malformed network URLs, e.g. `"http://[[REDACTED:ipv6]"` raises `ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL`. That escapes the adapter as `ValueError`, not an `HttpError`/`OSError`, violating the documented “Raises only `HttpError` subclasses” contract and defeating callers that migrate by catching `OSError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:require_http_url

chunk_findings.detail: The `except urllib.error.HTTPError` handler catches every `HTTPError`, but urllib turns each non-2xx response into an `HTTPError` unless a redirect handler follows it. A server returning `304 Not Modified` is not followed, so with the default `raise_for_status=True` the adapter raises `HttpStatusError(status=304)` despite the module/class documentation and the unused `STATUS_ERROR_FLOOR = 400` saying `HttpStatusError` is only raised for status >= 400. This makes normal conditional GETs fail.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:UrllibHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: A server that sends a non-HTTP status line causes `http.client` to raise `http.client.BadStatusLine` (an `http.client.HTTPException`), but urllib wraps exceptions from `getresponse` in `urllib.error.URLError`. `_classify` checks `URLError` first and returns `HttpConnectionError`, even though the module explicitly classifies “an answer that is not valid HTTP” as `HttpProtocolError`. Example: an HTTP endpoint responding `b'not-http\r\n'` is mislabeled as `kind="connection"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:_classify

chunk_findings.detail: `_get` selects the client with `(client or default_client())`. The `HttpClient` protocol imposes no truthiness contract, so a valid client implementation whose `__bool__` returns `False` (for example a recording fake that reports false when it has no responses) is silently ignored and `default_client()` is used instead. That makes the optional injection point unreliable and can cause a real network request in code or tests that explicitly supplied a fake; it should be `client if client is not None else default_client()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/release_index.py:52

chunk_findings.detail: A slow remote URL that accepts the TCP connection but never responds will make `HttpClient.request` raise `TimeoutError` (the chat path in this same file still catches `TimeoutError` explicitly). `TimeoutError` is an `OSError` subclass, not an `HttpError`, so this handler does not run and the timeout propagates to the caller instead of returning `False` as the old `except (urllib.error.URLError, OSError)` did. That changes behavior and can crash a review discovery when a checked URL times out.

chunk_findings.detail: The fake reuses the scripted `HttpResponse` (or at least its `reply.headers` dict) for every matching request. For example, after scripting `c.when("GET", "http://x"); r1 = c.request("GET", "http://x", timeout=5); r1.headers["X"] = "Y"; r2 = c.request("GET", "http://x", timeout=5)`, `r2.headers["X"]` is now `"Y"` instead of the scripted value. A real HTTP request would return a fresh response object; the fake lets a caller mutation of one response corrupt later responses from the same scripted rule.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/http.py: FakeHttpClient._answer

chunk_findings.detail: The `request` method never closes the caught `urllib.error.HTTPError` file-like object. After reading `exc.read(...)`, it either raises `HttpStatusError(...) from exc` (so `HttpStatusError.__cause__` holds the unclosed HTTPError) or returns a response; in both cases the underlying `http.client.HTTPResponse`/socket can remain open until garbage collection. A concrete scenario: repeat `request("GET", url, timeout=1)` against a server returning 500; each call can leave an open socket/file descriptor because the HTTPError body may be only partially read under `max_bytes` and is never closed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:request except urllib.error.HTTPError path

chunk_findings.detail: `require_http_url` calls `urllib.parse.urlsplit(url)` without guarding `ValueError`, and the call happens before the `try/except` in `request`. For `url = "http://[[REDACTED:ipv6]"`, `urlsplit` raises `ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL`. `request` therefore raises `ValueError`, not an `HttpError`/`OSError`, contradicting the class contract that `request` raises only `HttpError` subclasses; callers that catch `OSError` as promised will not catch this.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:require_http_url

chunk_findings.detail: The module doc and `STATUS_ERROR_FLOOR` state that urllib raises `HTTPError` only for status >= 400, but `urllib.request.HTTPErrorProcessor` raises for any non-2xx response not converted by the redirect handler, including 304 Not Modified. Thus with `raise_for_status=True` (the default), `request` raises `HttpStatusError` for statuses below the documented 400 floor. Concrete input: a conditional GET with `If-None-Match` that receives 304 produces `HttpStatusError`, contrary to the contract advertised here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:STATUS_ERROR_FLOOR

chunk_findings.detail: The new handler order puts `except HttpProtocolError` before `except OSError`. Python's `http.client.RemoteDisconnected` is both an `OSError` (via `ConnectionResetError`) and an `http.client.HTTPException`; the new `HttpProtocolError` is the adapter's HTTPException family. An endpoint that accepts the TCP connection and then closes before sending any status line therefore no longer reaches the old `"unreachable: ..."` branch and instead becomes `"bad HTTP exchange with the endpoint: ..."`. This is a caller-visible behavior change for a real transport condition and can change retry decisions based on the `unreachable` marker, violating the stated “no behaviour change for callers” contract.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `on_connect` handoff is performed before the fake has matched or evaluated the configured rule, so the fake reports a connected socket even when the request is configured to fail with a connection error. For example, `fake.when("GET", "http://x", error=HttpConnectionError)` followed by `fake.request("GET", "http://x", on_connect=cb)` appends a `FakeConnection` and invokes `cb`, then raises `HttpConnectionError`. A real client would not call `on_connect` for a pre-connect failure such as connection refused, and the added comment explicitly says the callback is called “once the socket is connected.” Tests that use the fake to verify abort/connection behavior can therefore observe a connected handle for a request that never connected, masking real failures or making false assertions pass.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/http.py:FakeHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts an exact ordering for the result of `_network_imports`, but `_network_imports` builds that result from `ast.walk`, which is documented to yield nodes in no specified order and, in CPython's current list-based DFS implementation, visits the last top-level statement first. For the concrete input `"import urllib.request\nfrom http.client import HTTPConnection\n"`, the `from http.client import HTTPConnection` node is processed before the `import urllib.request` node, so `_network_imports` returns `[("http.client", "HTTPConnection"), ("urllib.request", None)]`; the assertion expects the opposite list and fails. The test should compare sets/sorted lists or otherwise not rely on `ast.walk` ordering.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapters_http.py:test_the_blind_spot_check_sees_a_network_import_hiding_behind_an_allowed_root

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `on_connect` callback is invoked before the fake evaluates its rule error case, so a simulated connection failure still reports a connected socket. For example:

```python
client.when("GET", "http://example.com").error(HttpConnectionError("connection refused"))
seen = []
client.request("GET", "http://example.com", on_connect=seen.append)
```

This raises `HttpConnectionError` after `seen` already contains a `FakeConnection`. In the real client, `on_connect` is only called once a socket is connected, and a connection refusal has no connected socket, so the fake records a connection that never happened. The comment in the same change itself states that contract, but the implementation violates it for any pre-connect `HttpConnectionError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/http.py:FakeHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: `data` is only bound by `data = exc.read(max_bytes) if max_bytes is not None else exc.read()`. If that call raises the `http.client.IncompleteRead` the `except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException)` clause is meant to tolerate — e.g. a 500 response whose `Content-Length` promises a body but the server sends zero body bytes and closes — the exception is swallowed and `data` is never assigned. The subsequent `return HttpResponse(exc.code, headers_out, data)` (or `raise HttpStatusError(..., data)` with the default `raise_for_status=True`) then raises `UnboundLocalError`, escaping the adapter as a non-`HttpError`, so caller catch blocks for the documented contract are bypassed. Initialize `data = b""` before the try or turn the caught read failure into an `HttpIncompleteRead`/`HttpStatusError` instead of swallowing it.

With those files present, `test_no_module_outside_the_home_can_open_a_connection` passes even though both modules are outside the home and import `urllib.request`/`socket`, so the guard does not enforce “only the home imports them” and lets the reported architecture violation through. This is a caller-visible behavior change for a real transport condition and can change retry decisions based on the `unreachable` marker, violating the stated “no behaviour change for callers” contract.

chunk_findings.detail: The new baseline ignores `"ddflow.services.docscheck -> urllib"`, but the module touched in this same change is `ddflow/services/docscheck_net.py` (`ddflow.services.docscheck_net`), which is the module likely still using `urllib.parse`. Import-linter matches exact import graph module names, so an import from `ddflow.services.docscheck_net` is not covered by this entry, and the new `http-home` guard will fail on the unignored `ddflow.services.docscheck_net -> urllib` edge. The entry should be `"ddflow.services.docscheck_net -> urllib"` (or a separate `ddflow.services.docscheck` module must exist; the change’s manifest only shows `docscheck_net`).

chunk_findings.detail: `_network_imports` does not recognize the equivalent, allowed form `from urllib import parse`. A production file outside the home containing `from urllib import parse` produces `("urllib", "parse")`; in `test_no_module_outside_the_home_can_open_a_connection` the guard branches on `not mod.startswith("urllib.parse")`, so `"urllib"` does not match, and the tuple is not in `_ALLOWED_OUTSIDE_HOME`. The guard then reports it as an offender and fails, even though the same comment says `urllib.parse` is allowed anywhere.

chunk_findings.detail: The change claims the contract is that only the HTTP home (`ddflow/adapters/http.py`) imports `http.client`, but this test still directly imports `http.client` inside the function via `import http.client` and builds the cause with `getattr(http.client, exc)("nonsense")`. Since this file is under `tests/` and is not the HTTP home, a repository-wide import-linter http-home guard that covers the tests directory will flag this direct import, so the contract is not actually met. The test should use the already-added `FakeHttpClient` error alias form (as the incomplete-read test does) or a public adapter/ports constructor instead of importing the raw stdlib module.

chunk_findings.detail: The fake classifies every `HttpConnectionError` as a pre-connect refusal, but the adapter's confirmed classification maps post-connect `RemoteDisconnected` (and similar OS-level failures) to `HttpConnectionError`. If a test scripts `c.when("GET", "http://x", error=HttpConnectionError("http://x"))` and then calls `c.request("GET", "http://x", on_connect=cb)`, `_refused_before_connect` returns `True`, so `cb` is never invoked and no `FakeConnection` is recorded. A real client would have connected the TCP socket before the peer hung up, so the fake fails to model the `on_connect` hand-over for post-connect connection failures and can make tests pass even when the real adapter forgets to call `on_connect`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_refused_before_connect` treats every `HttpConnectionError` as a pre-socket refusal, but `HttpConnectionError` is the broad connection-failure family, not a specific pre-connect error. A scripted `HttpConnectionError` representing a reset or timeout that occurs after the socket is connected (for example, a peer that accepts the TCP connection and then drops before the response) will make `FakeHttpClient.request(..., on_connect=cb)` skip `cb`, even though the real adapter calls `on_connect` when the socket is handed over before surfacing that same failure. This makes the recording fake report that no connection was handed over for exactly the post-connect connection failures it is meant to emulate.

chunk_findings.detail: The change teaches the guard that `ddflow/infra/hostinfo.py` may import `socket`. `D-adapters-answers` makes `ddflow/adapters/` the HTTP home and says only the home imports `socket`; `ddflow/infra/hostinfo.py` is not that home. With an input tree still containing `import socket` in `ddflow/infra/hostinfo.py`, `test_no_module_outside_the_home_can_open_a_connection` will call this helper, get `True`, and therefore not report the offender, so the contract guard no longer enforces “only the home imports them” and an outside-home exception is blessed rather than shrunk.

chunk_findings.detail: `urllib.request.build_opener(_HTTPHandler, _HTTPSHandler)` passes the handler classes, not instances. `OpenerDirector.add_handler` expects an instance and invokes `handler.add_parent(self)`; when `handler` is a class this raises `TypeError` (`add_parent() missing 1 required positional argument: 'parent'`). Concrete input: `UrllibHttpClient().request("GET", "http://example.com", timeout=1, on_connect=lambda c: None)` crashes before any request is sent, so the socket-abort path is completely broken and the error is not an `HttpError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:_tracked_opener

chunk_findings.detail: `urllib.parse.urlsplit(url)` runs outside the `try` block and raises `ValueError` for malformed network URLs, e.g. `"http://[[REDACTED:ipv6]"` raises `ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL`. That escapes the adapter as `ValueError`, not an `HttpError`/`OSError`, violating the documented “Raises only `HttpError` subclasses” contract and defeating callers that migrate by catching `OSError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:require_http_url

chunk_findings.detail: The `except urllib.error.HTTPError` handler catches every `HTTPError`, but urllib turns each non-2xx response into an `HTTPError` unless a redirect handler follows it. A server returning `304 Not Modified` is not followed, so with the default `raise_for_status=True` the adapter raises `HttpStatusError(status=304)` despite the module/class documentation and the unused `STATUS_ERROR_FLOOR = 400` saying `HttpStatusError` is only raised for status >= 400. This makes normal conditional GETs fail.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:UrllibHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: A server that sends a non-HTTP status line causes `http.client` to raise `http.client.BadStatusLine` (an `http.client.HTTPException`), but urllib wraps exceptions from `getresponse` in `urllib.error.URLError`. `_classify` checks `URLError` first and returns `HttpConnectionError`, even though the module explicitly classifies “an answer that is not valid HTTP” as `HttpProtocolError`. Example: an HTTP endpoint responding `b'not-http\r\n'` is mislabeled as `kind="connection"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:_classify

chunk_findings.detail: `_get` selects the client with `(client or default_client())`. The `HttpClient` protocol imposes no truthiness contract, so a valid client implementation whose `__bool__` returns `False` (for example a recording fake that reports false when it has no responses) is silently ignored and `default_client()` is used instead. That makes the optional injection point unreliable and can cause a real network request in code or tests that explicitly supplied a fake; it should be `client if client is not None else default_client()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/release_index.py:52

chunk_findings.detail: A slow remote URL that accepts the TCP connection but never responds will make `HttpClient.request` raise `TimeoutError` (the chat path in this same file still catches `TimeoutError` explicitly). `TimeoutError` is an `OSError` subclass, not an `HttpError`, so this handler does not run and the timeout propagates to the caller instead of returning `False` as the old `except (urllib.error.URLError, OSError)` did. That changes behavior and can crash a review discovery when a checked URL times out.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test imports `http.client` directly to build `BadStatusLine`, but the HTTP adapter contract in this change says only the home module (`ddflow/adapters/http.py`) may import `urllib.request`, `http.client`, or `socket`. This non-home import adds a new architecture violator and can trip the `importlinter-http-home` guard or force the baseline to grow, which violates the “baseline ignore lists only shrink” constraint in [D-adapters-answers]. The test can pass an already-exported adapter exception or a locally constructed cause instead.

chunk_findings.detail: The contract for this change is that only the home module `ddflow/adapters/` imports `urllib.request`, `http.client`, or `socket`. The test `test_other_http_client_errors_are_named_and_never_retried_as_truncation` still has a direct `import http.client` inside it, so this file outside the home imports a low-level HTTP library. chunk_findings.detail: The new `on_connect` handoff is performed before the fake has matched or evaluated the configured rule, so the fake reports a connected socket even when the request is configured to fail with a connection error. For example, `fake.when("GET", "http://x", error=HttpConnectionError)` followed by `fake.request("GET", "http://x", on_connect=cb)` appends a `FakeConnection` and invokes `cb`, then raises `HttpConnectionError`. A real client would not call `on_connect` for a pre-connect failure such as connection refused, and the added comment explicitly says the callback is called “once the socket is connected.” Tests that use the fake to verify abort/connection behavior can therefore observe a connected handle for a request that never connected, masking real failures or making false assertions pass.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/http.py:FakeHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts an exact ordering for the result of `_network_imports`, but `_network_imports` builds that result from `ast.walk`, which is documented to yield nodes in no specified order and, in CPython's current list-based DFS implementation, visits the last top-level statement first. For the concrete input `"import urllib.request\nfrom http.client import HTTPConnection\n"`, the `from http.client import HTTPConnection` node is processed before the `import urllib.request` node, so `_network_imports` returns `[("http.client", "HTTPConnection"), ("urllib.request", None)]`; the assertion expects the opposite list and fails. The test should compare sets/sorted lists or otherwise not rely on `ast.walk` ordering.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapters_http.py:test_the_blind_spot_check_sees_a_network_import_hiding_behind_an_allowed_root

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `on_connect` callback is invoked before the fake evaluates its rule error case, so a simulated connection failure still reports a connected socket. For example:

```python
client.when("GET", "http://example.com").error(HttpConnectionError("connection refused"))
seen = []
client.request("GET", "http://example.com", on_connect=seen.append)
```

This raises `HttpConnectionError` after `seen` already contains a `FakeConnection`. In the real client, `on_connect` is only called once a socket is connected, and a connection refusal has no connected socket, so the fake records a connection that never happened. The comment in the same change itself states that contract, but the implementation violates it for any pre-connect `HttpConnectionError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/http.py:FakeHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: `data` is only bound by `data = exc.read(max_bytes) if max_bytes is not None else exc.read()`. If that call raises the `http.client.IncompleteRead` the `except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException)` clause is meant to tolerate — e.g. a 500 response whose `Content-Length` promises a body but the server sends zero body bytes and closes — the exception is swallowed and `data` is never assigned. The subsequent `return HttpResponse(exc.code, headers_out, data)` (or `raise HttpStatusError(..., data)` with the default `raise_for_status=True`) then raises `UnboundLocalError`, escaping the adapter as a non-`HttpError`, so caller catch blocks for the documented contract are bypassed. Initialize `data = b""` before the try or turn the caught read failure into an `HttpIncompleteRead`/`HttpStatusError` instead of swallowing it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:230 (UrllibHttpClient.request, except urllib.error.HTTPError branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The new home-boundary guard explicitly whitelists two imports that the stated contract forbids outside `ddflow/adapters/`: `ddflow/services/install_info.py` importing `urllib.request.url2pathname` and `ddflow/infra/hostinfo.py` importing `socket`. With those files present, `test_no_module_outside_the_home_can_open_a_connection` passes even though both modules are outside the home and import `urllib.request`/`socket`, so the guard does not enforce “only the home imports them” and lets the reported architecture violation through. This conflicts with [D-adapters-answers] and the intent’s home-boundary rule.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapters_http.py:_ALLOWED_OUTSIDE_HOME

chunk_findings.detail: The new `connected` flag is set from `opened`, which becomes true only after `_open()` has returned a response object. With the tracking opener, `on_connect` is handed the socket once the TCP connection is established; if the peer accepts the connection and then fails before any response is returned (for example it closes immediately, causing `http.client.RemoteDisconnected`, or times out before sending headers), the exception is raised inside the `with _open(...)` call before `opened = True` runs. `_classify` then produces a `HttpConnectionError`, and the new code sets `err.connected = opened`, i.e. `False`. A concrete input is a local socket that calls `accept()` and immediately `close()`s; `UrllibHttpClient().request("GET", "http://[REDACTED:ipv4]:port", on_connect=cb)` will invoke `cb` with a connected socket but raise `HttpConnectionError` whose `connected` attribute is `False`, contradicting the updated docstring that says `connected` means “the socket was up before it failed.” This also makes the fake diverge from the real client: a scripted `HttpConnectionError` with the default `connected=False` suppresses `on_connect`, while the real client can call `on_connect` for the same pre-response failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/http.py:UrllibHttpClient.request

chunk_findings.detail: `_pure_helper` only exempts `urllib.parse` and the two file-specific exceptions, while `_network_imports` treats every import whose top-level root is `http` as an offender. Given a module outside the home containing `from http import HTTPStatus`, `_network_imports` returns `("http", "HTTPStatus")`, `_pure_helper` returns `False`, and `test_no_module_outside_the_home_can_open_a_connection` fails, even though `http.HTTPStatus` is a pure status-code enum, not `http.client`, and is not “a way to open a connection” forbidden by the contract.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard hard-codes the HTTP home as the single file `ddflow/adapters/http.py` (via the exclusion `path != root / "adapters" / "http.py"` and message "only ddflow/adapters/http.py may open connections"), but [D-adapters-answers] states the home is the `ddflow/adapters/` directory. Therefore a future/current adapter under `ddflow/adapters/` (e.g. the next family's adapter) that legitimately imports `socket` or `http.client` would be listed as an offender and fail the test, falsely asserting a contract violation for code inside the permitted home. Fix should exclude `root / "adapters"` (the directory) or at least all of its files.
